conversation.content:
Hi there—I'm so glad you’re here. My name is Claire, and I’m a clinician who specializes in the emotional well-being of new mothers. I’m going to walk you through a short, evidence-based questionnaire called the EPDS (that stands for the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s simply a way for us to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, so we can make sure you’re getting any support you might need.  

Everything you share is completely confidential, and this is a judgment-free zone: no right or wrong answers—just whatever has been true for you over the past seven days. We’ll go through ten gentle questions; each one I’ll ask in everyday language so it feels like a conversation rather than a test. If at any point you’d like to pause or clarify anything, just let me know. Ready to begin?

First, I’m wondering: in the past week, have you still been able to enjoy the little things that used to make you happy, or does it feel as if the sparkle has gone out of life?

I mean… I still smile when I see my baby’s little yawns, and I’ll put on a favorite show while I fold laundry, but it’s like the color’s turned down. Things feel flatter—like I’m going through the motions more than actually feeling the joy I used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah, I can still laugh—like when my mom sent that silly meme yesterday—but it feels kind of quick and then it’s gone. I don’t get that warm, floaty feeling afterward like I used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do find myself thinking, “It’ll be nice when the weather warms up and we can take the baby for walks,” or “Maybe I’ll feel like baking again soon,” but the excitement part feels kind of muted—more “that could be okay” than a real flutter of looking-forward like I used to get.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… like yesterday the baby was extra fussy and I kept thinking maybe I ate something that bothered him, or I wasn’t holding him the “right” way. I know logically babies just have off days, but I still catch myself wondering if I missed some little thing I should’ve done better.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Every so often my heart races out of nowhere—like I’ll suddenly worry his breathing sounds weird even though it’s fine, or I’ll imagine tripping on the stairs while I’m carrying him. It usually passes if I take a few deep breaths, but it feels like my mind is always on “what-if” duty.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

I haven’t had full panic, but sometimes—especially at night when the house is quiet—my chest gets tight and I feel this wave of “something bad is about to happen.” I know it’s not rational, yet it still makes me double-check the baby monitor and pace the hallway until it fades.
Things have been getting on top of me

Mostly I keep things ticking over, but a couple of times this week—like when the diapers were running low and the laundry pile looked like Everest—I felt this flash of “I can’t keep up.” I take a breath, chip away, and I do manage, yet it’s that split-second sense of drowning that sticks in my head.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I wouldn’t say it’s outright unhappiness keeping me up—more just my mind spinning through tomorrow’s to-do list or replaying every little baby grunt. I usually drift off after an hour or so, but it’s definitely harder to settle than before he was born.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… there are stretches in the day when I just feel heavy, like a gray cloud parked over me. It’s not constant, but I’ve caught myself tearing up while washing bottles or staring out the window, wondering why everything feels kind of dim.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I’ve cried a couple of times this week—once when the baby wouldn’t latch and once when my partner asked how my day was. It wasn’t sobbing all day, more like tears slipping out when I’m already worn thin.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, nothing like that. I’ve felt low and tired, but hurting myself has never crossed my mind.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 15: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother, approximately 2–3 wks post-delivery (per clinical context)  
Date: ___  
Screener: Lic. Mental Health Professional  

Symptoms reported  
- Low mood (“gray cloud,” tearing up, crying while washing bottles)  
- Anhedonia (laughter feels “quick and gone,” anticipatory enjoyment “muted”)  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame for infant fussiness  
- Worry / physiological anxiety (heart racing, chest tightness, catastrophic “what-ifs” about infant safety)  
- Mild panic-like episodes at night with no clear trigger  
- Intermittent feeling “drowning” or “can’t keep up” with routine tasks  
- Initial insomnia secondary to racing thoughts; settles after ~1 h  
- No self-harm ideation (endorsed “no” on Q10)  

Patterns  
Mood and anxiety symptoms co-occur; worse at night; functional tasks still completed but with increased effort and distress. Insight intact (attributes symptoms to self, not infant).  

Screening significance  
EPDS equivalent items:  
- Items 8, 9 (sadness, crying) moderate endorsement  
- Items 3, 4 (anxiety, panic) moderate endorsement  
- Items 1, 2 (anhedonia) mild–moderate endorsement  
- Item 10 (self-harm) negative  
Overall pattern suggests elevated risk for postpartum depression with prominent anxiety features; adjustment difficulties and coping depletion present.  

Risk factors noted  
- Persistent low mood and crying spells  
- Sleep disruption linked to rumination rather than infant demands alone  
- Excessive maternal guilt / perceived incompetence  
- Recurrent intrusive worries and somatic anxiety  
- No safety concerns (denies self-harm)  

Screening observation  
Mother demonstrates subsyndromal but clinically significant depressive and anxious symptoms beginning within first month postpartum. Symptoms impair emotional well-being and sleep yet preserve basic infant-care functioning. Continue monitoring; consider standardized EPDS and further perinatal mood assessment; evaluate social support and psycho-education needs.
